entries.text: Home / About About & Education Graduate researcher in Engineering at Prairie View A&M University, working on functional materials, performance modelling, crystal growth, and magnetism. Research background My research examines how synthesis and processing change material structure and interfaces, and how those changes relate to physical response. I combine experimental characterization with physics-based modelling to study these relationships. My work with MXenes and related composites combines synthesis, processing, and characterization. I use MATLAB-supported thermal, photothermal, and electrochemical modelling to extract parameters and build interpretable links between measurements and response. My magnetic-materials research includes magnetic-powder synthesis, cobalt substitution in Mn1−xCoxGeTeO6 , and growth of Mn3Al2Ge3O12 single crystals. Visiting research appointments at Argonne and Los Alamos National Laboratories extended my experience in magnetic-domain analysis and single-crystal measurements. Before my graduate work, I studied Automobile Engineering at Thapathali Campus, Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University, Nepal. My earlier research covered biodiesel, plastic-derived fuels, nanoparticle additives, and engine performance, combustion, and emissions. entries.text: SUSTAINABLE ENERGY / BIODIESEL Biodiesel from diverse oils and fats I have prepared biodiesel from Jatropha seed oil, castor oil, palm oil, animal fat, soybean oil, sunflower oil, and waste cooking oil. My work explores the use of plant-based, animal-derived, and waste-derived feedstocks for alternative fuel preparation. Overview Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles Feedstocks used in my work The choice of oil or fat is an important part of biodiesel preparation. Feedstocks differ in composition, moisture, and free fatty acid content, which can influence pretreatment needs, conversion, and final fuel properties. Jatropha seed oil Castor oil Palm oil Animal fat Soybean oil Sunflower oil Waste cooking oil Understanding biodiesel preparation Biodiesel consists of fatty acid alkyl esters, commonly produced by reacting oils or fats with an alcohol through transesterification. The following stages outline the general preparation process; the treatment required depends on the feedstock. 01 / PREPARATION Feedstock preparation Oils and fats are prepared for conversion. Filtration removes suspended material, while moisture and acidity help determine whether further pretreatment is needed. 02 / CONVERSION Reaction and mixing During transesterification, triglycerides react with an alcohol to form biodiesel and glycerol. Mixing and temperature control are important aspects of the process. 03 / RECOVERY Separation and purification After reaction, product phases are separated. Further purification and drying help prepare the biodiesel for fuel-property evaluation. Inside the laboratory Photographs from feedstock handling and biodiesel preparation. Select an image to view the original. 01 / LABORATORY PREPARATION Heating and mixing setup Beakers and laboratory heating equipment used during biodiesel preparation, with a probe positioned in one vessel for monitoring. 02 / FEEDSTOCK HANDLING Waste cooking oil filtration Cloth filtration of waste cooking oil helps remove suspended food particles and other solid material before further processing. 03 / PRODUCT SEPARATION Biodiesel preparation and separation A laboratory demonstration of phase separation using separating funnels. Distinct liquid layers are visible during product recovery. 04 / FEEDSTOCK SOURCES Oilseed feedstock Oilseeds photographed during feedstock-related work, illustrating the plant-derived starting materials considered in biodiesel preparation. From preparation to fuel evaluation Preparing biodiesel is the first step towards understanding its suitability as an alternative fuel. Properties such as viscosity, density, acidity, and moisture content help characterise the product. Engine testing provides a separate assessment of performance, combustion, and exhaust emissions. entries.text: SUSTAINABLE ENERGY / ENGINE RESEARCH Combustion and Emission Experimental work on engine combustion, exhaust emissions, and smoke opacity. These photographs document laboratory testing, engine instrumentation, and the review of experimental measurements. Overview Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles 01 / ENERGY CONVERSION Combustion testing Combustion testing examines how fuel burns inside an engine and how chemical energy is converted into useful work. Cylinder pressure recorded against crank angle can be used to study combustion timing, pressure development, and heat-release behaviour. Engine speed, load, and fuel consumption provide additional context for comparing operating conditions and evaluating alternative fuel blends. 02 / EXHAUST CHARACTERISATION Emission and opacity testing Emission testing examines engine exhaust to understand the environmental effects of fuel use. Depending on the analyser, measurements may include carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen oxides. Smoke opacity testing measures how much light is blocked by an exhaust sample. It helps assess smoke behaviour and complements gas measurements; it is not a direct measurement of particulate mass. Inside the laboratory Engine testing, instrument checks, and experimental data review. Select a photograph to view the original image. 01 / ENGINE TEST FACILITY Research engine setup The engine test rig, instrumentation panel, and computer interface used for laboratory investigations of engine performance and combustion. 02 / COMBUSTION ANALYSIS Reviewing experimental measurements Collaborative review of engine test measurements at the data-acquisition workstation, connecting instrument readings with the interpretation of combustion behaviour. 03 / EMISSION TESTING Vehicle testing and instrument checks Preparation and inspection of testing equipment during a vehicle laboratory session. Instrument checks and consistent operating conditions support meaningful exhaust measurements. 04 / SMOKE OPACITY Instrument readings and record keeping Checking instrument readings and recording observations during engine laboratory work associated with smoke opacity testing. Connecting combustion with emissions Combustion and exhaust measurements provide complementary views of engine operation. Examining them together helps assess the relationships between fuel properties, operating conditions, energy conversion, and pollutant formation.

entries.text: Research / Scientific data analysis Scientific Data Analysis I analyse measurements from functional materials, crystal and magnetic studies, thermal experiments, and electrochemistry. MATLAB-supported processing, quantitative feature extraction, physical calculations, and statistical assessment connect measured signals with interpretable material descriptors and response parameters. Characterization Crystal & magnetic data Thermal & electrochemical Fit quality MATLAB workflow Engine analysis Research applications Materials characterization Each measurement requires its own processing choices. Baseline treatment, fitting constraints, normalization, and feature selection are retained alongside the extracted quantities. Measurement Analysis Quantities interpreted XRD Baseline correction and selected diffraction-profile fitting Peak position, basal spacing, width, area, and apparent stacking coherence Raman Corresponding-feature identification and spectral-profile fitting Frequency shifts, linewidths, and selected relative spectral contributions FTIR Baseline treatment and integration over defined spectral windows Band areas, band-area fractions, and lattice-normalized ratios XPS Survey quantification and constrained high-resolution envelope analysis Elemental ratios and relative chemical-envelope contributions Gas sorption Interpretation of surface-area and pore-analysis outputs Gas-accessible area, pore volume, and operational pore descriptors Zeta potential / DLS Comparison of electrokinetic and hydrodynamic measurements Zeta-potential magnitude and operational dispersion size SEM / EDX Morphology review and comparison of elemental-analysis outputs Observed particle or layer features, elemental distributions, and reported composition Explore characterization-derived descriptors → Crystal and magnetic-material data Structural and magnetic measurements are interpreted alongside composition, sample preparation, orientation, and measurement conditions. XRD & Rietveld refinement Phase identification, diffraction-profile comparison, and structural refinement support the interpretation of magnetic powders and crystalline materials. Magnetic measurements Comparisons retain field, temperature, sample orientation, and preparation history so that changes in measured response can be assessed in context. Magnetic-domain analysis Lorentz TEM analysis examines domain-related electron contrast and spatial magnetic features, retaining the imaging conditions used to interpret them. Single-crystal measurements My visiting research includes angle- and temperature-dependent dHvA measurements on HfSn₂ crystals. Sample orientation and measurement conditions remain part of the data context. Explore crystal growth and magnetic materials → Thermal and electrochemical analysis Thermal measurements Event selection and transient segmentation define which part of the measurement is being quantified. TGA / DTG: event boundaries, conversion, derivative peaks, and multi-rate comparison. Photothermal response: ambient correction, heating–cooling windows, amplitudes, time constants, and transient area. Reference calculations: keep directly measured quantities separate from calibrated or extrapolated estimates. TGA methods → Photothermal methods → Electrochemical measurements Potential, time, and frequency representations provide complementary views of the electrode response. CV: branch alignment, loop integration, background separation, and scan-rate comparisons. EIS: impedance components, phase, frequency-dependent capacitance, and consistency checks. GCD: charge–discharge segmentation, capacitance, charge balance, and energy integration. Electrochemical methods → Fit quality and physical consistency A fitted curve is one part of the analysis. Residual behaviour, parameter identifiability, uncertainty, and sensitivity are examined in the relevant modelling tasks. Residual structure Look for systematic deviations and temporal dependence that summary fit measures can conceal. Parameter identifiability Examine whether available measurements can distinguish the fitted parameters. Sensitivity Assess the effects of fitting windows, processing choices, and descriptor definitions. Uncertainty Use parameter intervals and resampling in the analyses where they are applicable. Model comparison Consider complexity, information criteria, stability, and appropriate withheld observations. Physical consistency Check units, limiting cases, sign conventions, and the plausibility of calculated quantities. Analysis choices follow the measurement and research question. Fitted parameters are interpreted with their units, assumptions, sensitivity, and physical consistency. MATLAB analysis workflow Organize Preserve raw files, sample identity, units, experimental settings, and acquisition metadata. Process Apply measurement-specific correction, interpolation, segmentation, or filtering, documenting the choices. Quantify Extract features, calculate integrals, apply physical definitions, and assemble comparison tables. Assess Check residuals, uncertainty, sensitivity, parameter stability, and physical consistency. Visualize Use clear axes, consistent units, meaningful normalization, and comparable scales. Interpret Connect the observations to the research question while retaining assumptions and experimental limits. Earlier engineering analysis My earlier engineering research and publications include alternative fuels, biodiesel blends, plastic pyrolysis oil, nanoparticle-assisted fuels, and engine testing. Analysis connects fuel preparation and operating conditions with performance, combustion, emissions, and thermal accounting. Explore related publications → Performance analysis Fuel-consumption, power, and efficiency calculations support comparisons under defined load, speed, and fuel conditions. Combustion analysis Combustion measurements and derived quantities are interpreted using the applicable engine protocol, acquisition settings, and calculation assumptions. Emission analysis Exhaust measurements are compared with consistent units, operating conditions, and instrument context. Concentration measurements remain distinct from mass-specific emission factors. Thermal-balance accounting Fuel-energy input, useful output, measured heat-loss terms, and the balance remainder support energy-distribution analysis. BSFC = ṁf / Pb ηb = Pb / (ṁf × LHV) Representative definitions: ṁf is fuel mass-flow rate, Pb is brake power, and LHV is lower heating value. Unit conversions and measurement conventions must be consistent. entries.text: Research / Modelling / Descriptor extraction Descriptor Extraction I extract interpretable variables from characterization measurements to describe material structure, surface chemistry, accessible interfaces, and dispersion. Baseline treatment, profile fitting, integration, and physical transformations connect each measured signal with a defined descriptor. The schematics below introduce the measurements and the meaning of the extracted quantities. XRD XPS Raman FTIR BET SEM / EDX Zeta XRD · Schematic Enlarge image Structural descriptors X-ray Diffraction Diffraction-profile modelling separates peak position, broadening, and area to characterize basal spacing and apparent stacking coherence. Basal spacing, d Interplanar distance obtained from Bragg’s law. Tracks spacing changes between corresponding reflections. Peak width, β Full width at half maximum. Describes broadening from coherence, strain, and instrumental contributions. Apparent Lc A Scherrer-type stacking-coherence estimate. Provides a comparative structural descriptor, rather than a direct flake-thickness measurement. Area / parent index Integrated intensity measures for selected regions. Track diffraction features without directly determining a residual-phase fraction. MATLAB: baseline correction → peak-profile fitting → residual assessment → structural descriptor extraction. XPS · Schematic Enlarge image Surface-chemical descriptors XPS Survey quantification describes surface composition. High-resolution envelope fitting examines relative contributions from selected chemical environments. Elemental ratios Quantified atomic-fraction ratios, including F/Ti where available. Describe relative surface composition. Binding energy Position of a fitted spectral contribution. Supports chemical-environment interpretation with calibration and assignment controls. Component fraction A component’s share of the fitted envelope area. Compares modelled chemical contributions within that region. TiOₓ-like fraction A model-dependent contribution associated with selected oxidized titanium environments. Fitting: background alternatives, constrained components, linked spin–orbit partners, and residual checks. Survey composition remains distinct from envelope fractions. Raman · Schematic Enlarge image Vibrational descriptors Raman Spectroscopy Corresponding vibrational features are fitted to quantify frequency displacement, broadening, and relative spectral contributions. Peak shift, Δω Frequency change relative to a defined reference. Tracks changes in the selected vibrational environment. Linewidth, Γ Width of a fitted vibrational feature. Describes broadening that can reflect disorder and other mode-dependent effects. Integrated area Signal beneath a fitted feature. Supports controlled comparisons of spectral contributions. Normalized shift Rescaled selected Raman shift. Supplies the vibrational variable used in the composite descriptor framework. MATLAB: spectral processing → corresponding-feature identification → peak fitting. Absolute intensity depends on acquisition conditions. FTIR transmittance · Schematic Enlarge image Integrated spectral descriptors FTIR Transmittance bands visualize infrared absorption. For descriptor extraction, corrected absorbance provides defined band areas and comparative spectral ratios. Band position Wavenumber of a selected absorption feature. Helps identify and compare vibrational regions. Band areas, B1–B4 Integrated corrected absorbance over defined windows. Quantifies each selected spectral contribution. B2 area fraction Relative contribution of the termination-sensitive region. Provides an interface-sensitive descriptor. Band-area ratios B2/B1, B3/B1, and B4/B1 compare termination-, adsorbate-, and hydroxyl-sensitive regions with the lattice-related window. Processing: when starting from transmittance, A = −log₁₀(T), with T expressed as a fraction. Baseline-corrected absorbance is integrated. The displayed schematic remains in transmittance. BET / gas sorption · Schematic Enlarge image Accessible interface descriptors BET & Gas Sorption Gas-sorption analysis describes accessible surface area and pore geometry. Derived variables provide inputs for interface and effective-transport models. Surface area, SBET Gas-accessible area per unit mass. Describes the interface available to the adsorptive probe. Pore volume, Vp Sorption-derived pore-space measure. Describes accessible pore capacity under the analysis assumptions. Pore diameter, Dp Operational pore-size descriptor. The approximation 4Vp/SBET connects pore volume and area under a defined geometric treatment. Interface area, av Surface area multiplied by an assumed bulk density. Provides a volumetric interface term for transport modelling. Interpretation: BET and pore-distribution analyses have distinct assumptions. Gas-accessible area does not directly determine thermally active interface area. entries.text: Research / Modelling / Electrochemical Electrochemical Modelling I model electrochemical charge storage through complementary analyses of cyclic voltammetry, impedance spectroscopy, and galvanostatic charge–discharge. The framework separates directly extracted descriptors, empirical rate relationships, and physical circuit models. MATLAB simulations connect resistance, storage, leakage, and relaxation times with complete measured curves. CV models EIS models GCD models Circuit simulation Model assessment MATLAB workflow CV · EIS · GCD — Schematic View full image Potential-controlled response Cyclic voltammetry Descriptor / Loop capacitance Integrate the complete response Anodic and cathodic branches are interpolated onto a common potential grid before integration. The potential window and scan rate remain explicit. This summarizes stored-charge response across the selected potential interval. C(ν) = [1/(2νΔV)] ∫VlowVhigh [ia(V) − ic(V)] dV ΔV = Vhigh − Vlow ν is the scan rate. ia and ic are corresponding branch currents. Specific or areal capacitance requires the corresponding mass or area normalization. Processing / Branch separation Separate common background current The branch average describes common-direction background, while the half-difference isolates the symmetric response used for rate analysis. A shared background can bias power-law fits performed on one branch alone. ibg(V) = [ia(V) + ic(V)]/2 is(V) = [ia(V) − ic(V)]/2 Cancellation applies to a contribution shared by both branches; it is not a universal separation of all electrochemical processes. Models / Scan-rate dependence Power-law and two-term analysis The power law describes current scaling. The Dunn-type decomposition represents terms proportional to scan rate and its square root. These provide operational rate descriptors for comparable potentials and measurement sessions. is(V,ν) = a(V)νb(V) is(V,ν) = k1(V)ν + k2(V)ν1/2 b describes rate scaling. k1 and k2 are operational decomposition coefficients. Conventional surface-like or diffusion-like interpretations do not prove a mechanism. Trasatti charge-accessibility analysis Slow- and fast-rate extrapolations provide operational outer and total charge estimates within appropriate fitting ranges. q(ν) = qout + c1ν−1/2 1/q(ν) = 1/qtot + c2ν1/2 The ratio qout/qtot is an accessibility descriptor. The validity of the extrapolation depends on the selected rate domain. Frequency-dependent response Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy Model / Equivalent circuits Describe resistance and relaxation Candidate networks combine series resistance, storage branches, and non-ideal capacitive elements. Circuit labels identify mathematical branches rather than predetermined mechanisms. These connect frequency dependence with interpretable resistance and timescale parameters. ZCPE(ω) = 1/[Q(jω)n] τRC = RC τR‖CPE = (RQ)1/n Q and n define the constant-phase element. Q is not directly a capacitance when n differs from one. Descriptor / Complex capacitance Re-express the measured impedance Complex capacitance supplies a complementary representation of storage and loss across frequency. Its interpretation remains tied to the impedance definition and any resistance correction. C*(ω) = 1/[jωZ(ω)] C*(ω) = C′(ω) − jC″(ω) Additional descriptors include the high-frequency real-axis intercept, low-frequency impedance, phase, and characteristic relaxation measures. Linear Kramers–Kronig checks and residual inspection support assessment of spectral consistency. A visually plausible circuit fit alone does not establish parameter identifiability. Current-controlled response Galvanostatic charge–discharge Descriptors / Time, charge, and energy Quantify resolved charge–discharge segments Segment duration, potential window, and applied current define apparent capacitance. Charge and energy integration provide complementary efficiency measures. These distinguish charge recovery from voltage-dependent energy recovery. Cchg = |Ichg|Δtchg/ΔV Cdis = |Idis|Δtdis/ΔV ηQ = |qdis|/|qchg| E = ∫VI dt Potential windows, resistive jumps, current signs, and normalization conventions are defined explicitly. Physical curve reconstruction From circuit topology to simulated response Within each multi-rate CV or GCD fit, one parameter set describes the complete family of curves. Rate dependence therefore emerges from circuit time constants rather than independent parameters assigned to every scan rate or current. Element Representation Purpose Rs Series resistance Ohmic contribution; constrained using EIS from the corresponding electrode. Ri ‖ Ci Relaxation branch Access-limited response with τi = RiCi. C3 Fully accessed storage capacitance Low-rate storage contribution. Rp Leakage path across the storage network Tests whether a conductive parasitic path is needed by the observations. CPE Distributed capacitive response Describes non-ideal relaxation over a range of timescales. Numerical model / State space Use capacitor voltages as states Finite RC networks are expressed as linear dynamical systems. The excitation changes between CV and GCD while the circuit equations retain their physical structure. This supports direct simulation of complete waveforms rather than only summary descriptors. dx/dt = Ax + bI V = cᵀx + DI x contains internal capacitor voltages. Matrices and vectors follow from the candidate topology. CV simulation: piecewise linear potential ramps For nonzero feedthrough D, potential control eliminates current from the state equations. Each linear sweep is propagated using the analytical linear-system solution. V(t) = V0 + st, s = ±ν I = (V − cᵀx)/D Initial state, cycle count, and sampling follow the experimental protocol. Analytical propagation avoids an arbitrary time-step approximation for the finite linear network. GCD simulation: constant-current segments Constant applied current drives the state equations. Charge and discharge segments are propagated to the defined potential boundaries, with switching and initial conditions retained explicitly. CPE realization: distributed timescales A CPE has no exact finite-dimensional state-space realization. I use a discretized relaxation-time distribution to construct a finite approximation over the experimental window. The numerical realization is checked against the analytical impedance before being used for time-domain simulation. Model choice and interpretation Separate empirical rate laws from circuit models. Empirical functions summarize capacitance versus scan rate or current. Circuit models instead aim to explain the complete curve family through shared physical parameters. Representative candidate rate laws C(x) = C0 C(x) = Ax−β C(x) = C∞ + Ax−β x denotes the relevant measurement rate. Here β is a fitted rate exponent, unrelated to TGA heating-rate notation. Model assessment considers parameter identifiability, bounds, residual structure, information criteria, bootstrap uncertainty, and withheld scan rates, currents, or frequencies. Extra circuit branches require support beyond improved visual agreement. Cross-technique comparison examines compatible resistance and relaxation scales. It does not assume that every technique must return identical apparent capacitance or share one independently untested fit. MATLAB implementation The modelling sequence. Import and check the measurements Preserve electrode identity, acquisition session, cycle selection, potential windows, scan rates, currents, and frequencies. Extract model-independent descriptors Calculate CV loop measures, branch-separated currents, impedance descriptors, and resolved charge–discharge quantities. Fit rate relationships Compare candidate functions using consistent observation windows and normalization. Construct candidate storage networks Compare blocking, relaxing, distributed, and leakage-containing topologies. Simulate the experimental excitation Apply piecewise potential ramps or current steps with the stated initial conditions and switching rules. Fit shared parameters within each curve family Let rate dependence emerge from the model rather than fitting independent parameters at every rate. Assess identifiability and predictive checks Examine residuals, parameter stability, bootstrap intervals, and appropriate withheld observations. Verify the numerical implementation Compare limiting cases with analytical RC and leaky-capacitor expressions, and check CPE approximations against analytical impedance. ← Back to modelling Electrochemical experiments →

entries.text: Research / Photothermal & Electrochemical Studies Electrochemical Studies I investigate electrode response through complementary measurements of current, potential, time, and frequency. Cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and galvanostatic charge–discharge provide connected views of charge storage, resistance, and relaxation. Research focus Techniques Comparison strategy Experimental workflow Research question How does the electrode respond across timescales? Electrochemical behaviour depends on the measurement timescale as well as the material. Complementary techniques help distinguish apparent charge storage, resistive contributions, and delayed access to the response. My approach compares complete measurement profiles alongside extracted quantities, including changes associated with cycling. Storage How much charge is accessed within the selected potential window and measurement duration? Relaxation Which response times influence frequency dependence and rate accessibility? Evolution How do measured profiles and derived quantities change across the defined cycling protocol? Complementary measurements Three techniques, different experimental questions. Quantities examined Loop shape, branch currents, integrated charge, apparent capacitance, and scan-rate dependence. EIS Impedance spectroscopy Measurement Small-signal response across frequency. Quantities examined Real and imaginary impedance, phase, resistance scales, and distributed relaxation. GCD Galvanostatic charge–discharge Measurement Potential evolution under defined current segments. Quantities examined Charge–discharge duration, apparent capacitance, charge balance, energy, and voltage changes. These techniques provide operational descriptors under defined conditions. entries.text: Research / Modelling Modelling & Descriptor Development My modelling work connects material characterization with thermal, photothermal, and electrochemical behaviour through interpretable descriptors, physical equations, and numerical analysis. MATLAB supports signal processing, parameter estimation, simulation, and model assessment. Each area below opens a dedicated page describing its methods, assumptions, and interpretation. Explore modelling methods Characterization to variables Descriptor Extraction Processing diffraction, spectroscopy, gas-sorption, and dispersion measurements to obtain structural, chemical, interfacial, and hydrodynamic descriptors. Methods include baseline correction, peak fitting, band integration, and physically defined transformations. XRD · XPS · Raman · FTIR · Gas sorption · SEM/EDX · Zeta potential · DLS Explore descriptor extraction → Thermal decomposition & conversion TGA & Thermal Kinetics Event-specific analysis of multi-rate TGA and DTG data, apparent activation-energy extraction, and numerical reconstruction of selected mass-loss events. The methods combine peak-based and isoconversional kinetics with an effective event model. TGA / DTG · Kissinger · FWO · KAS · Starink · Friedman Explore thermal modelling → Irradiation-driven temperature response Photothermal Modelling Mathematical treatment of laser-induced heating and cooling using transient energy balances. entries.text: Research / Modelling / Photothermal Photothermal Modelling Photothermal modelling translates measured heating and cooling curves into response times, thermal amplitudes, and reference-calibrated heat-input estimates. The analysis fits laser-on and laser-off segments separately and retains a clear distinction between measured, fitted, extrapolated, and reference-calibrated quantities. Energy balance Heating & cooling Calibration Extracted quantities MATLAB workflow The physical model Three terms describe the transient. A representative bulk temperature describes the suspension. Effective thermal capacity accounts for storage, while a combined heat-loss conductance describes exchange with the surroundings. Photothermal transient model · Schematic View full image → Heat input The effective rate of thermal energy supplied during irradiation. Thermal storage Energy accumulation associated with the changing system temperature. Heat loss Effective environmental loss proportional to the temperature rise. Csys dΔT/dt = Qin − HΔT ΔT = T − Tamb, H = hA Csys: thermal capacity, J K⁻¹ · Qin: heat-input rate, W · H: effective heat-loss conductance, W K⁻¹. Assumptions: representative bulk temperature, approximately constant thermal properties and laser input, effective linear heat loss, negligible evaporation, and cessation of irradiation-induced input at switch-off. Fit the two segments Heating and cooling tell different parts of the story. Laser on Heating response The fitted curve describes the approach toward an asymptotic rise under constant effective conditions. ΔT(t) = ΔT∞ [1 − exp(−t/τH)] τH: heating timescale. ΔT∞: model-extrapolated asymptotic rise. This form assumes zero initial temperature rise. For a nonzero initial rise, retain its exponential term. Laser off Cooling response Once irradiation ends, the temperature decays toward ambient through effective environmental loss. ΔT(t) = ΔToff exp[−(t − toff)/τC] τC: cooling timescale. ΔToff: rise at switch-off. The ideal lumped relation is τ = Csys/H. Heating and cooling times are fitted separately. The temperature reached at switch-off and the fitted asymptotic temperature are distinct quantities. An asymptote does not imply that equilibrium was reached during the experiment. Water-reference calibration Give the heat estimate a defined scale. Water cooling supplies a reference heat-loss conductance. Comparative sample calculations use that scale with explicit thermal-capacity assumptions. Csys = mliqcp + Ccontainer Hwater = Csys,water/τC,water Qnet,off = Hwater [ΔTsample,off − ΔTwater,off] The container contribution is not independently available and is set to zero in this calculation. The resulting calibration therefore uses nominal liquid thermal capacity. The switch-off estimator assumes compatible geometry and effective heat-loss behaviour. It remains distinct from equilibrium input or intrinsic conversion efficiency. Extracted quantities Each parameter has a specific meaning. entries.text: Research / Modelling / Physics-guided descriptors Physics-Guided Descriptor Modelling I connect material characterization with measured response through interpretable descriptors, explicit assumptions, and compact mathematical relationships. Characterization-derived variables are screened and normalized before they enter a response model. Physical reasoning guides their definitions, the candidate relationships, and the limits of interpretation. Framework Screening Descriptor families Response modelling Assessment MATLAB workflow The modelling framework From characterization to a physical question. My framework organizes characterization-derived variables before fitting response relationships. Physical reasoning guides the inputs, transformations, targets, and interpretation. Physics-guided descriptor framework · Schematic View full image → Characterization Extract structural, chemical, vibrational, porosity, and dispersion information. Descriptor construction Screen variables and construct explicit, interpretable material coordinates. Response modelling Compare compact relationships with concentration and selected material descriptors. Regression parameters remain estimated from observations. Physics supplies constraints and interpretation; this is not a first-principles calculation of optical absorption. Before the fit Screen the information entering the model. Check Question Why it matters Comparability Are the measured features physically equivalent? Prevents unrelated peaks or measurement definitions from being compared. Completeness Are inputs available and quantifiable? Missing and below-threshold values require explicit treatment rather than automatic zeros. Acquisition sensitivity Could instrument settings dominate the quantity? Limits reliance on uncontrolled absolute intensity. Redundancy Do variables repeat the same information? Reduces duplicated influence and unstable predictor combinations. Assumption dependence Is the quantity measured or model-derived? Separates independent inputs from assumed-parameter outputs. Circularity Was the variable derived from the response? Avoids reusing response information as an independent predictor. Material coordinates Three descriptor families, with explicit definitions. Normalize before combining Selected inputs are placed on a common scale. Feature direction and weighting are documented as part of the score definition. N(x) = (x − xmin) / (xmax − xmin) Ninverse(x) = 1 − N(x) Constant-valued features require exclusion or separately defined treatment. I Structure & interface Combines apparent stacking coherence, FTIR B2 band-area fraction, F/Ti, and pore diameter. I = [1 − N(Lc) + N(B2 fraction) + N(F/Ti) + N(Dp)] / 4 The inverted direction for Lc is an explicit choice in this score definition. D Vibrational features Retains a selected corresponding Raman-shift variable as a vibrational-change coordinate. D = N(selected Raman-shift variable) Distinct from linewidth-based broadening and a universal measure of disorder. S Dispersion Combines electrokinetic magnitude and operational hydrodynamic size. S = [1 − N(log10Dh) + N(|ζ|)] / 2 DLS size can include aggregates; it is not a direct sheet-width measure. These equal-weight scores are comparative within the defined material set, rather than universal constants. Defining I, D, and S does not require fitting all three together or establish a universal direction of performance. Explore the individual characterization descriptors → Response modelling Separate concentration from material information. Concentration describes an experimental condition. Material scores summarize characterization. Reduced candidate models keep those roles explicit. Qnet = β0 + βC ln(C/C0) + βSS Purpose: represent concentration dependence alongside a selected material descriptor. C0 is a reference concentration that makes the logarithm dimensionless. No fitted coefficients are displayed here. Compare candidate response shapes Linear, logarithmic, power-law, and saturation forms express different concentration dependencies. Physical motivation guides the candidates; model checks assess their support. Q(C) = QmaxC / (KC + C) This saturation candidate permits diminishing increments. A fit alone does not establish an optical or aggregation mechanism. Retain the energy balance Thermal storage, input, and loss define the physical meaning of the response target. Measured, fitted, and extrapolated quantities remain distinct. Csys dΔT/dt = Qin − HΔT ΔT∞ = Qin/H The equilibrium relation assumes constant effective input. A finite-time switch-off estimator is not silently substituted for equilibrium heat input. Assess the relationship Examine sensitivity, stability, and scope. Descriptor choices affect the relationship. Assessment examines alternative definitions, residual structure, parameter stability, and uncertainty alongside model complexity. Assessment Purpose Descriptor alternatives Compare FTIR fractions with ratios, pore measures, and linear versus logarithmic size transforms. Residual inspection Identify systematic behaviour the candidate model does not capture. Parameter stability Examine dependence on individual observations and correlated predictors. Complexity Limit adjustable terms to what the available material set can support. Uncertainty Track contributions from transient fitting, reference calibration, and descriptor construction. Validation scope Distinguish interpolation within measured conditions from prediction for new materials. Multiple concentrations of one material do not create multiple independent material descriptors. The number of distinct characterized materials limits material-level generalization. entries.title: Thermal Kinetics & TGA Simulation
entries.description: Explore multi-rate TGA and DTG analysis, Kissinger and isoconversional kinetics, activation-energy extraction, and MATLAB simulation of thermal events.
entries.headings: Start with mass loss and its rate. Express mass loss as conversion. Five techniques, two comparison strategies. Kissinger FWO KAS Starink Friedman From activation energy to a simulated event. The modelling sequence, step by step. Quantities carried into interpretation
entries.text: Research / Modelling / TGA Thermal Kinetics & TGA Simulation I use multi-rate thermogravimetric measurements to identify thermal events, extract apparent activation energies, and reconstruct event-specific mass-loss behaviour. The framework combines DTG peak analysis, isoconversional methods, and numerical integration for MAX, acid-etched MXene, and DMSO-treated MXene. TGA & DTG Conversion Kinetic techniques Simulation Major steps Multi-rate TGA · Schematic Enlarge Identify the thermal event Start with mass loss and its rate. TGA measures remaining mass as temperature increases. DTG highlights where mass loss occurs most rapidly, helping locate event boundaries and peak temperatures. Measurements at different heating rates allow the same event to be compared across temperature shifts. Corresponding events must be identified before estimating kinetic parameters. Derivative thermogravimetry DTG = −dm / dT With this sign convention, mass-loss events appear as positive peaks. Tp is the temperature of the selected DTG maximum. Normalize the selected event Express mass loss as conversion. Each selected thermal event receives its own initial and final mass references. Conversion then describes progress through that event rather than through the entire thermogram. Event-specific conversion α(T) = [m0 − m(T)] / [m0 − mf] α = 0 at the event start and α = 1 at its selected end. m0 and mf refer to that event’s boundaries. Non-isothermal kinetic equation dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)] f(α) β = dT/dt The Arrhenius term describes temperature dependence. f(α) represents the assumed conversion dependence. α Event-specific conversion β Heating rate, dT/dt T Absolute temperature in kelvin Ea Apparent activation energy A Apparent pre-exponential factor R Gas constant Compare kinetic descriptions Five techniques, two comparison strategies. Kissinger tracks the DTG peak. FWO, KAS, Starink, and Friedman compare measurements at a fixed conversion α, using the temperature Tα reached at each heating rate. Kinetic techniques · Schematic Enlarge Kissinger DTG peak-based analysis Tracks how the selected peak temperature changes with heating rate. Provides an apparent event-level activation-energy estimate. ln(β/Tp2) = C − Ea/(RTp) Plot: ln(β/Tp2) against 1/Tp. From slope s: Ea = −Rs. FWO Flynn–Wall–Ozawa · Integral isoconversional Compares heating rates at the same conversion without selecting a reaction-order function. Repeating the calculation across α gives an apparent activation-energy profile. log10β = Cα − 0.4567 Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: log10β against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs/0.4567. KAS Kissinger–Akahira–Sunose · Integral isoconversional Uses a temperature-corrected heating-rate transformation at fixed conversion. Complements FWO through a different integral approximation. ln(β/Tα2) = Cα − Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: ln(β/Tα2) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs. Starink Integral isoconversional Applies an alternative temperature-integral approximation. Provides another comparison of conversion-dependent apparent activation energies. ln(β/Tα1.92) = Cα − 1.0008 Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: ln(β/Tα1.92) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs/1.0008. Friedman Differential isoconversional Uses the conversion rate directly at fixed α. Supplies a differential comparison with the integral methods and requires careful derivative treatment. ln(dα/dt) = ln[A f(α)] − Ea,α/(RTα) dα/dt = β(dα/dT) Plot: ln(dα/dt) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs. C and Cα denote intercept terms. Temperature is expressed in kelvin and heating-rate units remain consistent. These methods estimate apparent kinetic quantities; agreement does not establish a unique mechanism. Reconstruct the measured event From activation energy to a simulated event. For event reconstruction, selected apparent activation-energy descriptors enter an effective first-order kinetic equation. The order is fixed at n = 1, while A is fitted separately for each experimental heating rate. General apparent event model dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)] (1 − α)n Effective first-order reconstruction: n = 1 dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)](1 − α) Numerically integrate over the selected temperature interval using the event boundary as the initial condition. Convert simulated conversion back to mass msim(T) = m0 − αsim(T)(m0 − mf) This reconstructs the mass change within the selected event. Multiple-event models require separately defined event contributions and mass-loss weights. Because A is fitted separately at each heating rate, this is an event-reconstruction test. It does not by itself demonstrate prediction at an unseen heating rate. The first-order form is an effective representation, rather than proof of first-order reaction chemistry. MATLAB workflow The modelling sequence, step by step. Import the multi-rate measurements Preserve mass, temperature, heating rate, sample identity, and acquisition conditions. Convert temperature to kelvin for kinetic calculations. Process the thermograms and calculate DTG Check the mass baseline and derivative sensitivity. Identify peak temperatures and candidate event boundaries. Match corresponding events Compare compatible transformations across heating rates. entries.text: Research / Two-dimensional materials MXenes & Functional Composites I study Ti₃AlCN-derived Ti₃CNTₓ MXenes and transition-metal sulfide composites, examining how processing changes their structure, surface chemistry, morphology, and functional response. My work combines synthesis and intercalation with complementary characterization, photothermal and electrochemical measurements, and physics-guided descriptor analysis. My primary MXene system Ti₃CNTₓ Layered titanium carbonitride MXene Tₓ denotes surface terminations introduced or modified during processing. About MXenes Processing Research questions Composites Characterization Functional studies The material family A layered framework with chemically active surfaces. MXenes are a family of two-dimensional transition-metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides. Their metal–carbon or metal–nitrogen framework is combined with surface groups that interact with surrounding molecules, ions, and other material phases. The family is studied for electrical conductivity, accessible surfaces, and tunable interlayer chemistry. In practice, performance depends on how the sheets are prepared, stacked, dispersed, and combined with other materials. Mn+1XnTx M An early transition metal; titanium in my primary material system. X Carbon and/or nitrogen within the layered framework. Tx Surface terminations, which can include oxygen-, hydroxyl-, and fluorine-containing groups depending on the preparation route. Material preparation Track the material through each processing state. I compare the precursor and processed MXene states so that structural, chemical, and functional measurements retain a clear preparation history. Ti₃AlCN MAX precursor The layered precursor supplies the starting structure and a reference for examining selective aluminium removal and subsequent material changes. Acid-etched MXene LiF/HCl etching is followed by centrifugation and washing to remove residual acid and soluble by-products. The recovered material is examined for changes in phase signatures, stacking, and surface chemistry. DMSO-treated MXene DMSO treatment promotes intercalation between layers. Washing and recovery prepare the treated material for comparisons of layer arrangement, dispersion, and measured response. Processing–structure relationships What changes when the layers are modified? Interlayer arrangement How do etching and intercalation affect basal spacing, stacking coherence, and the arrangement of layered assemblies? I use diffraction alongside complementary measurements to examine these questions. Surface chemistry How do surface composition and selected chemical environments change with treatment? Spectroscopic analysis helps distinguish surface-related contributions from changes in the underlying material framework. Dispersion & restacking How do the processed sheets assemble in suspension? Zeta potential, DLS, morphology, and gas-sorption measurements provide complementary information on dispersion and accessible interfaces. Structure & functional response Which measured structural and interfacial variables are useful for interpreting thermal stability, irradiation-induced heating, and electrochemical behaviour? Descriptor-based analysis connects these measurements while retaining their assumptions. MXene–sulfide systems A layered host with additional interfaces. My work also includes MXene-based composite systems containing transition-metal sulfides. These systems extend the research from modifying a layered material to examining how secondary phases are distributed and connected with it. NiS₂ CuS₂ ZnS MoS₂ The questions include phase identification, morphology, elemental distribution, and surface-chemical changes associated with composite preparation. The aim is to understand the interfaces rather than assume that combining materials automatically improves performance. Composite interpretation draws on XRD, Raman, FTIR, XPS, and SEM/EDS. Structural and spatial evidence are considered together when examining the relationship between constituent phases. Complementary measurements Build the material picture from several measurements. Each technique probes a different part of the system. I combine their information to examine structure, chemistry, accessible interfaces, dispersion, and stability. entries.text: Home/ Projects/ Undergraduate research Thapathali Campus · Undergraduate project · 2019 Testing of Performance and Emission Characteristics of Plastic Pyrolysis Oil and Jatropha Blend in IC Engines From fuel preparation to the engine test bench. A team investigation of diesel blends containing either plastic-derived oil or Jatropha biodiesel, connecting fuel properties with engine performance and smoke opacity. Explore the experimental work ↓ Institution Thapathali Campus Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University Programme Bachelor in Automobile Engineering Kathmandu, Nepal My role Undergraduate project team member Report submitted 11 August 2019 Study summary Abstract Adapted from the 2019 undergraduate project report for web presentation. An experimental investigation evaluated Jatropha biodiesel–diesel blends and Plasto diesel blends (PDB) through fuel-property measurements, engine-performance testing, and smoke-opacity assessment. Thermophysical properties were examined for JB20, containing 20% Jatropha biodiesel by volume, and PDB10, containing 10% plastic-derived fuel by volume. Engine tests covered Jatropha blends up to 20% and Plasto diesel blends up to 15%, with diesel as the reference fuel. The study compared indicated and brake power, thermal efficiency, specific fuel consumption, and fuel-consumption rate. The report found relatively small differences in brake power among the tested fuels and identified JB20 and PDB15 as promising blends within the evaluated performance measures. All tested blends were reported to pass the smoke-opacity test. Under the investigated conditions, the report described favourable performance of Plasto diesel blends relative to Jatropha blends. These findings apply to the blend fractions, equipment, and operating conditions evaluated in the project. The emissions comparison was limited to smoke opacity; NOₓ, SOₓ, HC, and CO were not measured. Experimental design Two fuel families. A diesel reference. Jatropha biodiesel + diesel JB5 · JB10 · JB15 · JB20 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% Jatropha biodiesel by volume; diesel makes up the remainder. Plasto diesel blend (PDB) PDB5 · PDB10 · PDB15 PDB means Plasto diesel blend. PDB5, PDB10, and PDB15 contain 5%, 10%, and 15% plastic-derived fuel by volume, respectively; diesel makes up the remainder. The reported engine comparisons treat these as separate blend series, each tested against diesel. Experimental workflow Preparation, measurement, comparison. Prepare the fuels Plastic processing involved batch-reactor pyrolysis, filtration, and fractional distillation. The Jatropha pathway used transesterified oil for biodiesel blends. Characterize the samples Fuel-property evaluation included density, viscosity, flash and pour points, calorific value, and cetane assessment. FTIR supported comparison of chemical signatures. Test against diesel Compare blend behaviour under engine loading, recording performance and fuel-consumption measures. Smoke testing provided a separate exhaust-opacity assessment. Interpret the response Examine how power, efficiency, fuel use, and opacity vary with blend fraction and test conditions, alongside the measured fuel properties. Test bench & analysis What was evaluated The performance-test setup was a single-cylinder, four-stroke, constant-speed, water-cooled diesel engine, rated at 3.50 kW at 1500 rpm, with a compression ratio of 18:1. Power & torque Indicated power, brake power, and torque as functions of engine load. Efficiency Indicated and brake thermal efficiency, mechanical efficiency, and volumetric efficiency. Fuel consumption Fuel-consumption rate and specific fuel consumption for the blend series and diesel reference. Smoke opacity Exhaust-smoke assessment using an RTM 430 opacimeter. Emissions measurement scope The project assessed smoke opacity. NOₓ, SOₓ, HC, and CO were not measured because a five-gas analyser was unavailable during the study. Plasto diesel blend (PDB) PDB5 · PDB10 · PDB15 PDB means Plasto diesel blend. PDB5, PDB10, and PDB15 contain 5%, 10%, and 15% plastic-derived fuel by volume, respectively; diesel makes up the remainder. The reported engine comparisons treat these as separate blend series, each tested against diesel.

entries.text: Experimental workflow Preparation, measurement, comparison. Prepare the fuels Plastic processing involved batch-reactor pyrolysis, filtration, and fractional distillation. The Jatropha pathway used transesterified oil for biodiesel blends. Characterize the samples Fuel-property evaluation included density, viscosity, flash and pour points, calorific value, and cetane assessment. FTIR supported comparison of chemical signatures. Test against diesel Compare blend behaviour under engine loading, recording performance and fuel-consumption measures. Smoke testing provided a separate exhaust-opacity assessment. Interpret the response Examine how power, efficiency, fuel use, and opacity vary with blend fraction and test conditions, alongside the measured fuel properties.

entries.text: Test bench & analysis What was evaluated The performance-test setup was a single-cylinder, four-stroke, constant-speed, water-cooled diesel engine, rated at 3.50 kW at 1500 rpm, with a compression ratio of 18:1. Power & torque Indicated power, brake power, and torque as functions of engine load. Efficiency Indicated and brake thermal efficiency, mechanical efficiency, and volumetric efficiency. Fuel consumption Fuel-consumption rate and specific fuel consumption for the blend series and diesel reference. Smoke opacity Exhaust-smoke assessment using an RTM 430 opacimeter. Emissions measurement scope The project assessed smoke opacity. NOₓ, SOₓ, HC, and CO were not measured because a five-gas analyser was unavailable during the study.
